annotation:
White exchanges, and opens up lines for his pieces. Unfortunately this reacts in Black’s favour, in accordance with the rule in these cases:
Open lines are to the advantage of the player whose development is superior.

metadata.Opening: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Desperately hoping that Black will snatch up the pawn by 12... Nxe4, when there would follow 13 Nxe4 Qxe4 14 R el, and the pin wins the queen.
But Black is not interested in grabbing pawns. His positional superiority is great enough to justify looking for a combination that will conclusively force a win. His bishops exert terrific pressure on their respective diagonals (even though one bishop is still undeveloped!). Each of them attacks a pawn shielding the king. Black’s queen is ready to swing over to the kingside, while the knight can leap in if more help is needed. Black controls the centre, a condition that, Capablanca says, is essential for a successful attack against the king. In short, Black is entitled to a winning combination as reward for his methodical positional play.
The question is: is there a target available for the explosion of this pent-up power?

metadata.Opening: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Covers the king’s flight-square, g1, and prevents him from returning there in answer to a check.
Black’s threat was 18... Qh3+ 19 Nh2 Qxh2#. As 18 Rxf2 runs into 18... Nxf2#, there was no escape.

metadata.Opening: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Practically forced, as Black was threatening 12...gxh3, as well as 12... g3.
White has managed to close the file, for the time being.

metadata.Opening: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Center Holding Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Desperately snatching at a loose pawn. In view of his retarded development and the plight of his king, such a capture is risky policy. If any hope remains it lies in some such move as 13 Be3. Not only does this bring another piece into play, but also in opposing one force with another of equal strength, it neutralizes the pressure of Black’s bishop. The text-move disregards the admonition:
Do not grab pawns at the expense of development or position.

metadata.Opening: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Center Holding Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: On the alternative 15 Bxb6 Black wins by 15...axb6 16 Kxh2 Qh4+ 17 Kg1 Rxg2+! (the fastest) 18 Kxg2 Bh3+! and White must either walk into mate by 19 Kg1 Qg5+ 20 Kh2 Qg2#, or into a discovered check by 19 Kh2 B xfl+ 20 K gl Bxe2, when the loss of material is ruinous.

metadata.Opening: Italian Game: Classical Variation, Center Holding Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must accept the sacrifice or lose rook and pawn for the knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: It would have been sounder strategy to retreat to e7 instead, where the bishop is invaluable for defence.

metadata.Opening: King's Gambit Declined: Classical Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Walking right into the teeth of the storm!
Before making a move that suggests itself so readily, Black might have asked himself, “How can I exploit White’s one weakness, the doubled pawns on the c-file?”
He might then have hit upon 12... Na5, with the object of swinging the knight to c4. There it blockades the doubled pawn, interferes with the free movement of White’s pieces, and in general sticks like a bone in the throat. White could capture the knight, but then he parts with one of his valuable bishops, and as a result of the exchange his pawn position would be inferior to Black’s. Finally, Black could then anchor one of his pieces to great effect on d5, a square from which it could never be evicted by pawns.

metadata.Opening: King's Gambit Declined: Classical Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: What else is there? Black tries to drive off the menacing knight. He cannot do this by 13... f6 as 14 d6+ Kh8 15 Nf7+ wins the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano, Greco's Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The king takes refuge in flight, incidentally unpinning the bishop and preserving his knight.
Spielmann’s strategy to this point and the decisive combination that follows would have pleased Lasker, who once said, “In the beginning of the game ignore the search for combinations, abstain from violent moves. Aim for small advantages, accumulate them, and only after having attained these ends search for the combination – and then with all the power of will and intellect, because then the combination must exist, however deeply hidden.”
A glance shows that White has achieved the requisite positional superiority. If there is a combination to be evolved, it must be now, before Black has time to reorganize his pieces for defence. Now, while he has five pieces actively in play against two of Black’s. Now, while he has an open file – enough! enough! The combination must be there!
Here is White’s line of reasoning:
Black’s advance of the g-pawn has deprived the knight of stable support. It is still guarded by two pieces, but if the bishop were not there it would be defended only once. In fact, if the bishop were not there, the knight would be pinned and subject to an enduring attack. The bishop appears in both equations. Obviously the bishop is the culprit, and it must be destroyed! And at once, before Black has time for 12... Be6!

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: No better is 17 ... Bxe5 18 dxe5 (uncovering the queen’s attack on the knight) 18... Bc8 (or 18. . . Bd5) 19 Rc7, when the miserable creature must perish.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king needs lots of room. The freeing attempt by 20... f5 loses to 21 Bxe6+ Kh8 (21 ... Kg7 22 Bh6+ wins the exchange) 22 Nf6 and resistance is hopeless.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only way to prevent 25 Bc5, after which White completely dominates the dark squares.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: What choice is there? If Black plays 11... h6 or 11... g6, he can never afterward play ...f6 without making the g6-square vulnerable to invasion by White’s pieces or the focal point of a sacrificial attack that would demolish his kingside.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: One lone pawn remains of the three which surrounded the king, and even that one is not long for this world.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White must preserve his valuable light-squared bishop.
Unfortunately, the time lost in being forced to make a pawn move is costly, as we shall see.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Better than this, which regains the pawn, is 14 Bg2 banishing the queen from the neighbourhood of his king.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This awkward move is absolutely necessary to save the g-pawn from 16... Nxe3 17 fxe3 Qxg3+. Should this pawn fall, his king could not withstand the attack.
White may have intended to play 16 Bc5, when after 16... Nf6 he could have put up a fight by 17 Rxf6 Bxf6 18 Bxf8, but at the last moment saw the refutation: 16... Bxc5 17 Nxc5 Nf6, and in order to stop 18... Ng4 and 19... Qh2#, he must give up his rook for the knight, a course which means an eventual loss.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A very good move! To begin with, it prevents Black playing 12... Nd5, to remove by exchange White’s attacking pieces. Offensively, it prepares an advance of the d4-pawn, which will break up Black’s pawn structure at e6. Once this is done, White’s rook will have a point of entry on the e-file.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This seems to win a pawn, as should White recapture by 14 cxd5 the reply 14... Nxd5 not only holds on to the pawn but compels an exchange of bishops, taking the edge off White’s attack.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
To prevent 19 Re3, and to give the bishop more play on the long diagonal.
How does White continue the attack? Can he bring up the reserves without losing too much time? Or can he weaken the defensive formation and make it vulnerable to immediate assault?
Is there a hint in the last question? Yes, indeed!
Black’s chief defence lies in his knight, which guards against the mate at h7, and the f-pawn supporting the all-important g-pawn. If only White could strike at these two defenders – threaten them, remove them, get them out of the way somehow...
There is a move, the kind that looks absurd at first glance!
Hint No. 2: A master player looks at every move he would like to make, especially the impossible ones.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Vacating a square for the king. Black abandons the projected 15... c5, against which Tarrasch intended (according to his own comments) 16 Qh3 (threatening 17 Bxf6) 16... h6 17 Bxh6 and now:
1) 17... c4 18 Bxg7 Kxg7 19 Qg3+ Kh8 20 Qh4+ Kg7 21 Qg5+ Kh8 22 Qh6+ (pretty zigzagging by the queen!) 22... Kg8 23 Re5 with a quick mate.
2) 17...gxh6 18 Qxh6 cxd4 (to meet 19 Re5 with 19... Rc5) 19 Qg5+ Kh8 20 Re4 and Black must give up his queen to avoid mate.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Hoping that 17 Bxf6 gxf6 18 Qxh7+, winning a pawn, will appease White.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s first dividend comes in the form of an open centre file leading straight to Black’s king!

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This move is superior to the natural 9 Re1+. It is, as we shall see, both energetic and subtle.
One finesse is directed against Black’s castling. After 9...0-0, White would play 10 Qd3 threatening 11 Qxh7#. Black would be forced to reply 10... g6 (not 10... f5 11 Qd5+ Kh8 12 Nf7+, winning the exchange) and weaken the defensive formation of pawns. Once the line of pawns is disturbed, the king is vulnerable to direct attack.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
An interesting move. In its retreat, the bishop not only attacks the knight but also manages to unblock the d-pawn.
Black hopes either to force the knight to leave or to bring about an exchange of pieces, ridding himself of the attacking knight.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black prefers this to 13... Kf8 imprisoning the h8-rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Looks good, as Black saves the a-pawn, keeps the queen out of b7, and prepares to double rooks and to supply the wretched pawn with another defender.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black attacks one of the pawns hemming in his queenside.
Against 20... Bf6 White sticks to the script with 21 f4, followed by 22 Be2 and 23 Bf3.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The defence 26... Qf6 succumbs to 27 e4! (now we see the point of 26 Qa2 – it is to pin Black’s e-pawn and prevent 27... e5 at this point) 27... R cd 8 28 e5 Qf4 29 Qc2 (threatening 30 Qh7+ Kf8 31 Bg6 Re7 32 Qh8#) 29... Qg5 30 f4 Qg4 31 Rc3, when the entrance of the rook at g3, followed by 33 Qh7+, is conclusive.
Notice that the move 31 Rc3, relaxing the pressure on the queenside, is not an infraction of principle. An attack that leads to a forced win takes precedence over positional considerations.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black protects his queen, which was threatened with capture. Other courses offer bleak prospects:
1) If 25... Qxd4 26 exd4 Bc8 (to save the a-pawn), then 27 Rxd5 wins a pawn for White.
2) If 25... Qb7, then 26 Qc5 followed by 27 a4 and 28 b5 engineers a decisive breakthrough.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: At last, the light-squared bishop comes into the game. Black’s move looks effective as mate is warded off, the enemy queen driven back, a piece developed, and another one (the a8-rook) released.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If Black sacrifices the exchange by 22... Rxe6 then he may prolong but not alleviate the suffering.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Hoping to induce an exchange of rooks which would divert one of White’s pieces from the attack. White could still win, but the play would require care. It might go like this: 21 Rxa6 Bxg5 22 Qxg5 Bxa6 23 Rf6 (23 Bxg6 at once is risky and might even lose) 23...cxb2 24 Bxg6 fxg6 25 Rxg6+ Kf7 26 Rg7+ Ke8 27 Qe5+ Kd8 28 Qb8+ Bc8 29 Rxd7+ Kxd7 30 Qxb2, etc.
But Pillsbury is not to be swayed! He carries out the motif of the attack with admirable consistency by annihilating the g-pawn that stepped out of line and weakened the defensive formation.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: To prevent 15... Ng4, an invasion by another piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The king takes a hand in the ending, making its way in along the weakened light squares.
Tarrasch’s recipe in similar cases is “The king must be moved (in the ending) as far as is compatible with his safety, right into the enemy camp, where he can capture pawns, hold up hostile pawns and lead his own pawns on to queen.”
Reuben Fine says clearly and simply, “The king is a strong piece – use it!”

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black’s plan becomes manifest: he wants to force an exchange of knight for bishop. This would leave bishops commanding squares of different colours on the board, which often exerts a drawish influence on the game.
Another alternative worth considering was 19... Nb7 in order to play 20... c5 and get his central pawn phalanx rolling.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: And now an attack on the pawn...

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: ...which can only be met by further retreat!

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
No better was 24... Kd6 to back up a pawn push, as the reply 25 Kd4 nips that little idea in the bud.
Black’s best chance was with 24... Rf8, to get some counterplay by getting his h8-rook into the game by way of the open file. The move he does make attacks the bishop and succeeds in its object of driving it away from a good square – but only on to a better one!

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A shot at the bishop, to force its retreat. Meanwhile, Black gains time for the development of his own bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The bishop withdraws – but not to d3, where an attack by 12 ... Nb4 enables Black to bring about an exchange of knight for bishop. White wants to preserve the bishop, which has excellent prospects for attack when it emerges later at d3 or f3.
[ Editor’s Note: 12 Nxd5 exd5 13 Bd3 wins an important pawn for nothing – brutal but effective.]

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: After 18... Kc8 19 Kf3 (threatening 20 Re8+ Kb7 21 Rdd8 winning a piece) 19... Nf6 20 Re7 Rf8 White can either attack on the kingside by 21 g4 or start his pawn phalanx on the queenside rolling by 21 a3 followed by 22 b4.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Putting the pawn under lock and key. It cannot advance, and White’s intended stratagem of manoeuvring his queen over to b7 is not feasible, Black’s reply to 32 Qb4 being simply 32... Rxc6. But the very fact that one pawn can keep Black’s queen and rook occupied is a tribute to the power of a passed pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is running out of good moves. He rejects 26 Qe2 as the reply 26... Rc2 leads to further exchanges. An attack on the pinned knight by 26 Rea1 is cleverly met by 26... Qb5, nimbly extricating the knight from danger.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest response, as the recapture will give White an isolated pawn in the middle of the board.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not only to support his own passed pawn but to bring the queen into active play.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White hopes to complicate matters, as 31 Rxc2 is not attractive.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Triple attack on the e-pawn! This forces White either to defend the pawn tamely, or else to go ahead boldly with the combination he planned.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White blockades the d-pawn and prepares to advance his own passed pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight leaps to d5 and attacks pieces all over the place! It threatens one bishop directly (by 22 Nxb4) and the other indirectly, by 22 Nxf6+ gxf6 23 Rxd7. In addition to this, it threatens 22 Nc7 , attacking both rooks and thereby winning the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black does what he can to keep the enemy rook out and seals up all the entrances.
White has the superior position, but how does he break through?
Let us listen in on what Rubinstein might say to himself in reasoning out a course of action:
My rooks are as well placed as they can be and doing a good job in controlling the open d-file. My queen is strongly centralized and exerts pressure in every direction. My bishop bears down on his e-pawn and keeps a rook and knight chained to its defence. My pieces are all usefully occupied and must stay where they are.
How about my opponent? His defence just about holds together, but his pieces must stay where they are to guard his weak points. If I leave him alone, he might consolidate his forces, and even counterattack.
If I leave him alone...
Say, isn’t that the key to the position?
I must not leave him alone! I must interfere with the arrangement of his pieces. I must drive them off from their present positions. In fact, I might ruin his game by driving off even one defender!
Since my pieces are all useful where they are, I must not disturb them but look to my pawns to break up the defence. Which pawn shall I use, and which of his pieces shall I try to dislodge?
The first thing to do is to find a target. His queen and rooks are too far away and too agile to be bothered by pawns. Any of them can move off to a different square on a file or a rank and still control it. I must aim at a fixed target – some piece that is needed at the spot where it is stationed and loses its effectiveness as soon as it is displaced. How about the knight? Suppose I played 29 h4 and gave it a nudge by 30 h5? It would have to leave its fine defensive position immediately. Where could it go? If to e7, it blocks the action of the e8-rook, and if it retreats to the back rank, it is out of play for a time. Besides, I get another benefit in moving the h-pawn. It gives my king a flight square, so that he doesn’t fall into a surprise mate on the first rank.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Simple and strong! The queen makes a powerful entrance at d5, seizing control of a diagonal leading to the king and at the same time tripling heavy pieces on the open central file. Notice the admirable use of d5 as a pivot for the manoeuvring of the various pieces. It has been occupied in turn by knight, bishop, rook and queen – aptly enough, in order of strength!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Hoping for safety in the corner. If instead 30... Rf7, then 31 h5 Nh8 32 h6 decisively breaks up Black’s defensive pawn wall, or if 30... Kf8, then 31 h5 Nh8 32 Rd8 Nf7 33 Rxe8+ Kxe8 34 Qe6+ Kf8 35 h6 Re7 (nothing else saves the game, as 35... Nxh6 allows mate on the move, and 35...gxh6 36 Qxf6 leads to ruin for Black) 36 Qc8+ Re8 37 hxg7+, and White wins a rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This move not only evicts the knight from its strong defensive post but also drives a wedge into Black’s position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black gets his knight back into active play and prevents White from striking again at the f-pawn by 33 Bh4. He side-steps the pretty loss 32...gxh6 33 Rxf6 Rd7 34 Bxe5! Rxd5 (if 34... Rxe5, 35 Rxf8+ and mate next move) 35 Rxf8# – double check and mate!
